adds.title: Diversidad sexual en Madrid - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Madrid-specific LGBT page documents Madrid as one of Europe's main LGBT hubs and backs the record's route-3 claims about scene visibility: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2005, Madrid Pride (MADO), held annually in late June/early July, is described as one of the largest Pride events in the world drawing millions of attendees, and the Chueca district is the epicentre of the community. It also records local institutions: COGAM, founded 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation, Madrid's city government runs an Oficina de Atencion a la Diversidad Sexual y de Genero, and Arcopoli focuses on fighting discrimination and violence. Crucially for a traveler assessment, the article states that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in Madrid and that marginalised LGBT groups, such as migrants and trans people, face additional barriers.

adds.title: Ley trans (España) - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
adds.summary: This Spanish Wikipedia page on trans law is the national-framework document the Madrid region record stands under: it records that the Comunidad de Madrid was among the first Spanish regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and Region de Murcia (following Extremadura in 2015), which is the 2016 regional statute that Ley 17/2023 later amended. It also covers the state-level Ley 4/2023 (Organic Law of 28 February 2023) on gender self-determination and the framework with which regional statutes like Madrid's must comply, giving the statutory floor a trans traveler in the region stands under.

adds.title: LGBTI en France - Wikipédia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBTI en France' page is the framework document every French region, Bourgogne-Franche-Comté included, stands under: the law of 17 May 2013 opened marriage to same-sex couples, and the article details legal protections against discrimination while stating that LGBT people continue to be the target of discrimination and violence, with reports of such incidents rising. Its transidentité section covers the legal framework for gender recognition in France. This supplies the national legal baseline (marriage, anti-discrimination law, gender recognition) that applies identically in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, against which the region's own documented restriction (the Dijon Pride march ban) is an exception rather than the rule.

adds.title: Marche des fiertés en France - Wikipédia
adds.summary: This page on Pride marches in France documents, citing France 3 Bourgogne, that from 2013 pride marches were organised in the Bourgogne cities of Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre - i.e., the Dijon march that the Côte-d'Or prefecture banned from the city centre in June 2025 was an established regional event with over a decade of local history, not a first-time gathering. The page also records the nationwide growth of marches since the mid-1990s (with marches spreading to provincial cities from 1994-1995 onward), providing the French regional context in which the Dijon restriction occurred.
